Well, there’s not a set answer to that.  To forget trauma is an incredibly complex phenomenon, and a traumatic memory is not only a memory but an encoded experience.  We know from neuroscience that there are neurobiological systems that allow the brain to process traumatic experiences and encode them into long-term memory, and this is helpful in learning from the experience and staying safe from similar threats in the future.  

However, this doesn’t mean that these memories are stable and unchanging, particularly if the experience is negative.  Memory can be erased, or re-stored, or be “modulated” by repeated experiences in a new context.  For example, a child who repeatedly learns that being hit by his parents is bad, and that his parents are un-loving, can start to re-code these experiences to be encoded differently.  It’s possible for a child to re-learn that his parents are good people, and that they love him, and if that is repeated over enough time, then the memory may be modified in such a way that the original trauma is forgotten or softened, and the child is able to build a stable and more positive relationship with his parents, in an age-appropriate way.

chosen: The body’s normal internal temperature is around 98.6 degrees F, and this is regulated by a complex feedback system involving the brain, hormones, blood vessels, and the skin. Heat is produced by the body’s metabolism, and this heat is dissipated by the blood circulation, which carries it to the skin, where it’s released to the environment. When the body starts to get too cold, the brain triggers the release of hormones that constrict the blood vessels in the skin, and increase heat production. When it gets too hot, the sweating mechanism is activated, and blood vessels in the skin dilate to release heat to the environment. External Heat Loss:  The body can lose heat via conduction, convection, and radiation.  For example, the skin is a very important organ of heat loss, since it makes up almost 3/4 of the body’s surface and is a massive heat transfer organ.  When the ambient temperature becomes too hot, the body sweats to increase surface area and radiative heat loss.  When the ambient temperature becomes too cold, the body shivers to increase its insulation, and in very cold situations will actually start shivering uncontrollably to generate body heat and keep the core temperature up.

External Heat Gain:  The body can also gain heat from the environment, through conduction, convection, and radiation.  For example, warm clothing keeps the body warm by reducing radiative heat loss, and sitting by a fire increases heat conduction throughout the body.  When these heat transfer processes are too great, the body regulates temperature by moving to a cooler location or shedding excess clothing.

Internal Heat Production and Loss:  The body also regulates its temperature through internal mechanisms.  This includes the basic metabolic processes in the body, which generate heat.  Additionally, the body regulates its temperature by sweating, shivering, vasodilation, vasoconstriction etc.  As the body gets too hot internally, it uses these thermoregulatory mechanisms to shed excess body heat.  Likewise, when the body gets too cold internally, it will generate more heat through shivering and other thermoregulatory processes to fight off the cold.  

The body is a remarkably efficient machine, and takes many different mechanisms to regulate its temperature and maintain a generally comfortable internal core temperature.  Heat loss mechanisms tend to be more active when the body is too hot, and heat production mechanisms are more active when the body is too cold.

The Wading River is a very small river in New York, located in the town of Shawangunk along the Shawangunk Ridge.  The river only flows throughout the winter season, and is named for the boggy conditions it flows through in the surrounding region.  The Wading River is only a few miles long, and joins the Wallkill river at Wallkill.  The river is formed by the confluence of four small tributaries, namely the Pond Brook, Barbell Brook, Smith Brook, and Black Brook.  The Barbell Brook, in particular, contains several scenic waterfalls, one of which is known as Barbell Falls.  
The Wading River is fully contained within Shawangunk National Wildlife Refuge, and has been designated a New York State “Coldwater Fishery”, which indicates that the river has a naturally cold water temperature and contains healthy populations of trout and other coldwater species.  The Wading River  also has notable eel and bass populations, as well as a substantial populations of other aquatic life such as blue claw crabs, crayfish, and bullhead catfish.  A number of rare plant species are also known to grow along the river, including the Bog Algae (Fontinalis antipyretica), horned pondweed (Zannichellia palustris), and Twinflower (Linnaea borealis).  The areas around the Wading River are also historically notable due to the presence of numerous prehistoric artifacts which have been found along the river.

chosen: I think your question assumes there are certain important qualities of “reading a book” that are always true, no matter what the medium.  However, I don’t think this is true, and there are important qualities of book reading that are better (or worse) in different contexts.  If the main quality you care about is “how much text can be read in the time available”, then on average, a book has more text than an e-book, but an e-book has more text than a text message.
prompt: What difference, if any, is there between reading a book on a kindle, iPhone or paper book?
rejected: As you may know, the Kindle and the iPhone are both computerized devices, while a paper book is a physical, non-digital object.  Some differences include that a book on the Kindle is downloadable, and thus more easily transported, and will “auto-save” when you stop reading, but a physical book can be lent to a friend, and can be rescued if the device were to break, etc.  A physical book is also more likely to be passed down to the next generation of readers, if it survives.  Additionally, the content on a kindle is often full-color, but a physical book is in black and white.  The latter two differences are simply differences in presentation, though, while some content on the Kindle is in black and white, other content is full-color, like photographs.  Also, content on a physical book can be written in many languages, while content on the Kindle is often in English only.  Some Kindle content is available in a number of different languages, though.
